delivery_risks.title: Client Review done twice
delivery_risks.summary: One consulting engagement (case for the client identified in the log) went through the Client Review stage twice within about two weeks — first on 2026-05-04 with one consultant, then again on 2026-05-18 with a different consultant. Both review entries ended in the same unresolved state, 'awaiting partner sign-off'. Across the live event log, 2 cases show this repeated-review pattern. The review is being held more than once and is not reaching a completed, signed-off outcome on the first pass. Root cause: First-pass client reviews are not being brought to a conclusion — they stall waiting for partner sign-off and are handed to a different consultant, so the review has to be repeated rather than confirmed and closed.

evidence.label: avg_delay_days
evidence.detail: measured across 3 case(s) at Client Review

delivery_risks.recommended_action: Make the first Client Review a confirm-and-close step by preparing sign-off in advance and keeping the review with one owner.
action_steps: Circulate a short findings summary to the client and the signing partner two working days before the review so the meeting confirms conclusions rather than uncovering new questions.
Assign a single named consultant as owner of each engagement's review, so it is not re-run by a second person when it stalls.
Build the partner sign-off into the review itself — have the partner attend or pre-approve against the summary so the case does not sit 'awaiting sign-off' after the meeting.
Only re-book a second review by explicit exception, with a recorded reason, rather than as the default when sign-off is outstanding.

delivery_risks.title: Cases stall entering Proposal
delivery_risks.summary: Cases reaching the Proposal stage are waiting on average about 19.3 days before the proposal is completed. Only 3 cases were detected, and the log shows those proposals do eventually reach a 'Complete' or 'Done' status, so the issue is the length of the wait rather than proposals being dropped. The evidence supplied is thin — it confirms the delay and that the cases resolve, but does not itself reveal whether the wait comes from slow drafting, missing paperwork, or a client-side approval sitting outside the firm's control. Root cause: Proposals sit for roughly three weeks because the firm has no fast, repeatable way to produce and progress them — drafting starts from scratch and/or waits on inputs the firm does not track — so each proposal accumulates avoidable idle time.
delivery_risks.recommended_action: Speed up proposal turnaround with reusable templates and clearer handoff data captured earlier.
action_steps: Build a small set of costed proposal templates for the firm's common engagement types, so drafting becomes filling in scope and rates rather than writing from scratch.
At the Qualification stage, capture who on the client side signs off and their expected timeline, and record it on the engagement row.
Track proposal wait time and split it into 'firm-side drafting' versus 'waiting on client', so the true source of the 19.3-day delay becomes visible.
Review the 3 affected cases to confirm which portion of the delay is internal drafting versus external approval before scaling the fix.

delivery_risks.title: Cases loop back to Delivery
delivery_risks.summary: The live event log shows the Delivery stage being entered more than once for a small number of cases — two cases loop back into Delivery rather than moving forward to Client Review. Both affected deliveries were handled by the same team member, and the recorded statuses (one 'sent', one 'done') suggest work was marked complete but then had to be revisited. The volume is small (2 cases), so this is an early or isolated signal rather than a systemic breakdown. Root cause: Delivery work is being treated as finished and then reopened, most likely because the scope or client expectations were not locked down before delivery, so completed work has to be redone.
delivery_risks.recommended_action: Lock scope and a single point of contact before delivery, and pause any reopened work until a change is formally agreed.
action_steps: Confirm and document the agreed deliverables and acceptance criteria at Onboarding, before Delivery starts, so 'done' means the same thing to consultant and client.
Name one decision-maker per engagement and route all delivery requests and sign-off through that person to prevent conflicting instructions.
When a delivered item comes back, raise a short change note that records what changed and pauses further delivery until the revised scope (and fee, if applicable) is agreed.
Review these two cases with the consultant who handled them to see whether the reopening came from unclear scope, changed requirements, or a quality gap, and record the reason.

past_resolutions.resolution: Delivery reopened repeatedly on one account because the sponsor kept adding stakeholders who each wanted something different. Named a single decision-maker at onboarding and routed all requests through them. Effective on that account; harder to enforce with public-sector clients.

Work went back into delivery after review because the brief changed mid-engagement and nobody re-priced it. Introduced a change note that pauses delivery until the revised scope and fee are agreed. Scope changes stopped being absorbed silently.

Invoices were raised late because the practice manager waited for the consultant to confirm the work was finished. Set a standing rule that a completed milestone is invoiced on the Friday of that week. Billing lag fell from three weeks to under one.
